Cut down or quit cold turkey? How to taper nicotine pouches

There is no single right way to quit nicotine pouches or snus. Health services describe two: cutting down first, or stopping completely on a set day. Here is how each works and how to choose.

Short answer. Sweden's health service 1177 suggests cutting down over about three to four weeks, so your brain gets used to less nicotine, and then stopping on a set date. Norway's Helsenorge says some people prefer to quit cold turkey, while others pick a quit date two to four weeks ahead. Either way, on the quit day you stop completely.

Option 1: stop on a set day

You pick a date and stop using pouches completely from that day. Withdrawal is usually worst in the first two to three days and mostly fades within a few weeks (see the withdrawal timeline).

To prepare, Helsenorge suggests:

  • choosing a quit date two to four weeks ahead;
  • changing where and when you use pouches before then, and practising short stretches without them;
  • thinking ahead about hard moments, like parties, stress or the drive to work, and making "if this happens, I'll do that" plans.

Option 2: cut down first, then stop

1177 recommends starting with the pouches you need least, cutting down over about three to four weeks and then setting a quit date. There are two ways to step down, and you can combine them:

  • Fewer pouches a day. Lower your daily limit a little every week.
  • Lower strength. Move to a weaker pouch, for example from 6 mg to 3 mg, before stopping.

The milligrams on the can tell you how strong a pouch is, not exactly how much nicotine gets into your body. Use them to compare products, not to count doses.

Some people use nicotine-free pouches for a while to keep the habit of something under the lip, and 1177 mentions them as a step. Helsenorge notes that they can still irritate the gums, depending on what's in them.

Nicotine replacement and medicines

Nicotine replacement can take the edge off withdrawal. Helsenorge lists gum, patches, lozenges, mouth spray and pouches sold as medicines, and says to use the recommended dose: too weak a dose for too short a time makes a relapse more likely.

For people quitting snus, the Norwegian guideline says nicotine replacement raised short-term quit rates and eased cravings, and one study found that the prescription medicine varenicline raised quit rates. A 2025 Cochrane review of 43 trials found that varenicline and counselling probably help people quit smokeless tobacco, and nicotine replacement may help.

Talk to a pharmacist or doctor about what suits you, especially if you're pregnant, take other medicines or have a heart condition.

How to choose

  • If you want it over quickly and can clear a few hard days, a set quit day keeps things simple.
  • If you have tried stopping overnight before, or you use a lot of strong pouches, cutting down first can make the quit day less of a shock.
  • Either way, set a quit date. 1177 suggests setting one even when you cut down first, so the taper has an end.

After a slip

One pouch doesn't wipe out your progress. Note what led to it, such as alcohol, stress or a certain place, plan for it next time, and carry on from where you are.

Free help

US: 1-800-QUIT-NOW and the free EX Program. Sweden: Sluta röka-linjen, 020-84 00 00. Norway: the free Slutta app from Helsenorge. Denmark: Stoplinien, 80 31 31 31.
